scenes.tts: Dig up a soybean plant and look at its roots. You find small round bumps. Cut one open, and an active one is often pink inside. These bumps are packed with bacteria. Most of us learn the word bacteria next to the word germs. So, are bacteria and viruses always harmful?
scenes.visual: A soybean root with round bumps; one is cut open, pink inside, with bacteria dots; ends on a question: germs or partners?

scenes.tts: Living things use nitrogen to build proteins and D N A. The air is mostly nitrogen gas. Plants and animals cannot use it in that form. Nitrogen fixation changes nitrogen gas into a form living things can use. Only some bacteria and archaea can do this.
scenes.visual: Nitrogen gas blocked from plants and animals; a bacteria chip converts it into usable nitrogen, which feeds proteins and DNA

scenes.tts: In soybeans, these bacteria live inside a nodule. A nodule is a small swelling on a root. The bacteria turn nitrogen gas into ammonium, and the plant uses it. The plant sends the bacteria energy-rich food from photosynthesis. When both species benefit, we call it mutualism.
scenes.visual: Nodule with bacteria; nitrogen gas in, ammonium out to plant, food from plant back; both benefit

scenes.tts: Now picture a stream full of fallen leaves. A decomposer breaks down dead plants, animals and wastes. Bacteria and fungi do most of this work. They release enzymes that break large molecules into smaller ones. The nutrients return to the soil or water. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up, and its nutrients would stay locked inside.

scenes.tts: Your gut holds trillions of bacteria. This community is your microbiome. Gut bacteria break down fiber by fermentation, which works without oxygen. A pathogen is a microbe or virus that causes disease in its host. The host is the living thing it lives in or on. E. coli usually lives quietly in your large intestine. Some strains cause illness when they get into food or water.

scenes.tts: Viruses matter too. A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria. In a lab model ecosystem, a virus infected an ocean alga. Bacteria then broke down the dead algae. The water gained nitrogen and phosphorus that other living things could use. So, are bacteria and viruses always harmful? No. Whether a microbe helps or harms depends on which microbe it is, and where it lives.
